insights.title: Nu handles 23.6% of card spending — but only 15.5% of card lending
insights.takeaway: Nu's customers already spend through Nu far more than they borrow through Nu. If Nu turned spending into lending at Itaú's rate, it would hold ≈ R$17bn more in card loans — without winning a single new customer.

insights.detail: For every 1% of Brazil's card spending Nu handles, it captures only 0.66% of card lending; Itaú converts at 0.75. Nu's rate has been improving (0.55 in 1Q23 → 0.66 now), so the gap is closing — but what's left is worth ≈ R$17bn at today's market size. This is the cleanest way to measure how much lending growth Nu can get from customers it already has.

insights.title: Nu's biggest share jump ever happened while the card market was shrinking
insights.takeaway: In 2Q25 Brazil's total card loans fell -2.3% and Itaú cut its book -5.9% — yet Nu grew +8.2%. Result: Nu's largest single-quarter share gain on record (+1.41pp).

stat.label: market share gained in one quarter (2Q25) — a record — while the market shrank

insights.detail: Growing when the whole market grows proves little — you're just riding the tide. Growing while the market shrinks means Nu was lending exactly when the big banks were pulling back from card risk. Two possible readings: Nu's data lets it spot good borrowers the incumbents can't — or Nu is taking on the risk the incumbents wanted off their books. How Nu's 2025 loans repay over the next year will settle which one it was.

insights.title: Nu's loan menu is riskier than the big banks' — before skill even enters
insights.takeaway: 97% of Nu's book is credit cards + personal loans — Brazil's two highest-default products. Give every bank IDENTICAL skill and Nu's book would still run 10.1% defaults vs 8.2% for Itaú and 7.3% for Bradesco. That's risk built into WHAT Nu sells, not HOW WELL it lends.

stat.label: the default rate Nu's product menu alone implies — vs 8.2% Itaú / 7.3% Bradesco

insights.detail: Comparing banks on headline default rates mixes up two different things: what products they sell, and how well they pick borrowers. This calculation strips out the first. Practical use: when Nu reports defaults close to the big banks, it is actually out-lending them by roughly this gap; when Nu's defaults look worse, check how much is just the menu before drawing conclusions. It also prices the payroll push — every 1% of the book moved from cards into payroll trims ~6.2bp (hundredths of a %) of built-in risk.

insights.title: Nu's default premium is 2.1pp, not 3.7pp — once you compare the same kind of loans
insights.takeaway: Headline NPL says Nu (6.9%) runs +3.7pp above the big three (3.2% average). Strip the incumbents down to their HOUSEHOLD books — the only part comparable with Nu — and the premium falls to +2.1pp. 43% of the scary gap was book mix.

stat.label: Nu's real default premium over incumbent household books (2Q26)

insights.detail: This is the single biggest correction to make when reading Nu's credit numbers. Itaú's 1.9% whole-bank ratio is held down by mortgages and corporate lending; on households alone it prints 3.7%. Nu has no such ballast, so its group ratio IS its household ratio. What survives the adjustment is a genuine premium — Nu still lends to a riskier household than Bradesco does — but it is 2.1pp, and it should be judged against Nu's pricing (see the price-of-risk insight), not against a number built from a different balance sheet.
insights.formula: headline premium = Nu NPL − average incumbent whole-bank NPL;  like-for-like premium = Nu NPL − average incumbent HOUSEHOLD NPL;  mix effect = the difference

insights.title: Nu prices personal loans +43.2pp above Itaú, and carries +12.3pp more cost of risk
insights.takeaway: On the one product both report comparably, Nu charges 105.5% a.a. against Itaú's 62.3%. Across their whole books, Nu's credit losses run 15.1% a year against Itaú's 2.8%. The pricing premium is the bigger of the two numbers — the higher default rate is bought, not simply suffered.

stat.label: Nu's personal-loan pricing premium over Itaú (2Q26), against a +12.3pp cost-of-risk premium

insights.detail: Every "Nu's NPL is high" argument is incomplete without the other side of the trade. Nu prices its personal lending far above the incumbents and books far higher credit losses; both are visible here, and the pricing gap is the larger. What this cannot tell you is the margin: the rate is one product's APR on new lending while cost of risk covers each bank's entire book, so the two must be read side by side rather than netted. For the actual spread you would need Nu's realised asset yield, which this workbook does not carry. The structural risk is the same either way — what happens if Brazil caps rates, or if losses rise faster than Nu can reprice.
sources: Personal Loans - Interest rates sheet (BCB weekly, % a.a.)

insights.title: Card defaults at a record 10.0% — but NEW defaults aren't rising
insights.takeaway: The scary headline — a record 10.0% of card loans gone bad — describes OLD loans still sitting on banks' books. The share of loans just starting to miss payments is 3.0%, +0.1pp vs a year ago and unremarkable by its own history.

stat.label: change vs a year ago in NEW card defaults — the number that describes today's borrowers

insights.detail: Think of a bathtub: the headline default rate is the water level; new defaults are the tap. The level is at a record, but the tap is flowing no faster than last year. That means the level comes from old problem loans aging on the books (and banks writing them off slowly) — not from today's borrowers getting into trouble. For judging Nu — whose book is ~64% cards — the tap matters more than the level.
sources: BCB credit data workbook (NPL & Early NPL sheets, monthly %)

insights.title: Nu is sprinting into payroll loans just as the big banks walk out
insights.takeaway: Nu's payroll-loan book (loans repaid straight out of salaries) grew +180% in the year to 2Q26, while Santander's sits -21.5% below its peak. On the all-payroll average it's Nu's safest product — but private-sector payroll now defaults at 10.6%, above credit cards, so which borrowers Nu lends to decides whether this waters risk down or adds to it.

stat.label: growth in Nu's payroll loans in the year to 2Q26 — from a 0.29% share to 0.73%

insights.detail: Payroll loans get deducted from paychecks before the borrower can spend the money, which is why they run 2.6× fewer defaults than credit cards — even now, at the product's worst-ever 3.8%. The timing is the story: Nu scales in exactly when a big incumbent retreats and the product's defaults peak — a classic contrarian entry. And it connects to the 'loan menu' insight: every 1% of Nu's book that shifts from cards to payroll trims about 6.2bp of built-in risk.

insights.title: Private-sector payroll defaults more than doubled in 9 months — to 10.6%, above credit cards
insights.takeaway: Payroll loans — repaid straight out of salaries — are the textbook safe product, and for public employees (2.7%) and INSS pensioners (2.2%) they still are. But private-sector payroll defaults went from 5.0% in Nov 2025 to 10.6% in Aug 2026, above credit cards (10.0%). Its early-warning gauge is 1.7× last year's level, so more is already in the pipeline.

insights.detail: A payroll deduction is only as good as the payroll behind it. A public salary or an INSS pension keeps paying through a downturn; a private-sector deduction is only there while the borrower keeps the job. That is why the all-payroll average (3.8%) is the wrong number for judging a payroll book: it blends a 2.2% INSS segment with a 10.6% private one. For Nu this matters directly — payroll is its fastest-growing product (see the payroll insight), and whether that growth lowers or raises its risk depends on which of these three lines it is lending into.

insights.title: Inter is the proof: 'being digital' isn't the edge — being Nu is
insights.takeaway: Brazil's other listed digital bank gained just +0.24pp of card share in two years while Nu gained +2.35pp — 10× more. Meanwhile Inter's defaults sit 3.1pp above Itaú's — the furthest they have ever been.

stat.label: Nu gained 10× more card share than Inter over the same two years

insights.detail: If a slick app and no branches were all it took, Inter would be compounding like Nu. It isn't: barely any share progress, and loan quality drifting the wrong way while Itaú sits at its best-ever default rate. For a Nu investor this cuts both ways. It confirms Nu's edge is specific to Nu — funding cost, data, execution. But it also removes the comfort of a sector tailwind: Nu has to keep out-executing, because 'digital' by itself demonstrably doesn't win.
